nameStory: This lichen gets its 'medallion' name from its circular, coin-like appearance when viewed from above, resembling decorative medallions or ancient coins scattered across tree bark. The 'Frost's' part honors Edward Tuckerman Frost, though it was actually first described by the renowned American lichenologist Edward Tuckerman himself in the 1800s.
description: Frost's Medallion Lichen is a crusty, circular lichen that forms small, coin-sized patches on tree bark. Like all lichens, it's actually a partnership between a fungus and algae working together as one organism. These grayish medallions typically measure less than an inch across and create distinctive circular patterns that look almost stamped onto the bark surface. It's quite rare in New England, being much more common in the warmer southeastern United States.

idTips.label: Circular Growth Pattern
idTips.description: Forms distinct medallion-like circles on bark, with well-defined rounded edges that feel slightly raised and crusty to the touch

idTips.label: Gray Coloration
idTips.description: Displays pale gray to whitish colors, sometimes with subtle greenish tints when moist, contrasting noticeably against darker bark

idTips.label: Crusty Texture
idTips.description: Surface feels rough and brittle when dry, like old paint or dried plaster, and may crack in geometric patterns

idTips.label: Bark Preference
idTips.description: Found exclusively on tree bark, never on rocks or soil, typically on hardwood trees with relatively smooth bark

idTips.label: Size Range
idTips.description: Individual medallions stay relatively small, usually under an inch in diameter, though multiple colonies may grow near each other

habitat: In New England, this southern species is extremely rare and would most likely be found on the bark of hardwood trees in warmer, protected locations such as urban areas or south-facing slopes. Look for it in mixed deciduous forests or along forest edges where temperatures are milder. Given its southeastern distribution, any New England sightings would likely be in the warmest microclimates of southern Connecticut or Rhode Island.

seasonality.spring: Medallions may appear slightly greener and more vibrant as moisture returns, making the circular patterns more noticeable against awakening tree bark.
seasonality.summer: Peak visibility when dry conditions make the crusty, coin-like appearance most pronounced and the gray coloration contrasts sharply with bark.
seasonality.fall: Still visible and identifiable, though may blend more with changing bark colors and accumulated debris on tree trunks.
seasonality.winter: Remains present year-round as lichens don't go dormant, though snow and ice may obscure the medallion patterns on lower trunk sections.

funFact: This lichen is like a tiny weather station - it can actually absorb water from fog and humidity in the air, not just from rain, allowing it to survive in surprisingly dry conditions where most plants would perish!
confusionNotes: Could be confused with other crusty gray lichens on bark, but the distinctive medallion or coin-like circular growth pattern is unique - remember 'medallion' and look for those perfect circles rather than irregular splotches.
contextualKnowledge: The rarity of this species in New England means any sighting would be quite significant - it's primarily a southeastern species that may be expanding its range northward with climate change, making it an indicator species worth documenting.
compareHints: Since this is the only Dirinaria species recorded in New England, compare it with other crusty bark lichens in the button lichen family. Unlike many related species that form irregular patches, Frost's Medallion maintains its characteristic circular, coin-like appearance. Other crusty lichens tend to spread in more random, irregular patterns without the defined medallion borders.
